      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span>, Male</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Although <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is much more common in women, men can get it too. It happens most often to men between the ages of 60 and 70.</p><p><span class="qt0">Breast</span> lumps usually aren't <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. However, most men with <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> have lumps. Other <span class="qt0">breast</span> symptoms can include:</p><ul><li>Dimpled or puckered skin</li><li>A red, scaly nipple or skin</li><li>Fluid discharge</li></ul><p>Risk factors for male <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> include exposure to radiation, a family history of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, and having high estrogen levels, which can happen with diseases like cirrhosis or Klinefelter syndrome.</p><p>Treatment for male <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is usually a <span class="qt0">mastectomy</span>, which is surgery to remove the <span class="qt0">breast</span>. Other treatments include radiation, chemotherapy and/or hormone therapy. </p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/breastcancer.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Paget's Disease of <span class="qt0">Breast</span></content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt0">Breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer is a cancer</span></span> that starts in <span class="qt0">breast</span> tissue.  It happens when cells in the <span class="qt0">breast</span> change and grow out of control. New cells grow even when you don't need them, and old cells don't die when they should. These extra cells can form a mass called a <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tumor</span></span>.</p><p>Sometimes the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> does not spread any further. This is called "in situ." If the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> spreads outside the <span class="qt0">breast</span>, the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is called "invasive." It may just spread to nearby tissues and lymph nodes. Or the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> may metastasize (spread to other parts of the body) through the lymph system or the blood.</p><p><span class="qt0">Breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is the second most common type of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> in women in the United States. Rarely, it can also affect men.</p>What are the types of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>There are different types of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. The types are based on which <span class="qt0">breast</span> cells turn into <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. The types include:</p><ul><li>Ductal <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">carcinoma</span></span>, which begins in the cells of the ducts. This is the most common type.</li><li>Lobular <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">carcinoma</span></span>, which begins in the lobules. It is more often found in both <span class="qt0">breasts</span> than other types of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Inflammatory <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer, in which cancer</span></span> cells block lymph vessels in the skin of the <span class="qt0">breast. The breast</span> becomes warm, red, and swollen. This is a rare type.</li><li>Paget's disease of the <span class="qt0">breast</span>, which is a <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> involving the skin of the nipple. It usually also affects the darker skin around the nipple. It is also rare.</li></ul>What causes <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p><span class="qt0">Breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> happens when there are changes in the genetic material (DNA). Often, the exact cause of these genetic changes is unknown.</p><p>But sometimes these genetic changes are inherited, meaning that you are born with them. <span class="qt0">Breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> that is caused by inherited genetic changes is called hereditary <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>There are also certain genetic changes that can raise your risk of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, including changes in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. These two changes also raise your risk of ovarian and other <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span>.</p><p>Besides genetics, your lifestyle and the environment can affect your risk of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>The factors that raise your risk of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> include:</p><ul><li>Older age</li><li>History of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> or benign (noncancer) <span class="qt0">breast</span> disease</li><li>Inherited risk of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, including having BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene changes</li><li>Dense <span class="qt0">breast</span> tissue</li><li>A reproductive history that leads to more exposure to the estrogen hormone, including:
	<ul><li>Menstruating at an early age</li><li>Being at an older age when you first gave birth or never having given birth</li><li>Starting menopause at a later age</li></ul>
</li><li>Taking hormone therapy for meopause</li><li>Radiation therapy to the <span class="qt0">breast</span> or chest</li><li>Obesity</li><li>Drinking alcohol</li></ul>What are the signs and symptoms of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>The signs and symptoms of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> include</p><ul><li>A new lump or thickening in or near the <span class="qt0">breast</span> or in the armpit.</li><li>A change in the size or shape of the <span class="qt0">breast</span>.</li><li>A dimple or puckering in the skin of the <span class="qt0">breast</span>. It may look like the skin of an orange.</li><li>A nipple turned inward into the <span class="qt0">breast</span>.</li><li>Nipple discharge other than <span class="qt0">breast</span> milk. The discharge might happen suddenly, be bloody, or happen in only one <span class="qt0">breast</span>.</li><li>Scaly, red, or swollen skin in the nipple area or the <span class="qt0">breast</span>.</li><li>Pain in any area of the <span class="qt0">breast</span>.</li></ul>How is <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> diagnosed?<p>Your health care provider may use many tools to diagnose <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> and figure out which type you have:</p><ul><li>A physical exam, including a clinical <span class="qt0">breast</span> exam (CBE). This involves checking for any lumps or anything else that seems unusual with the <span class="qt0">breasts</span> and armpits.</li><li>A medical history.</li><li>Imaging tests, such as a mammogram, an ultrasound, or an MRI.</li><li><span class="qt0">Breast</span> biopsy.</li><li>Blood chemistry tests, which measure different substances in the blood, including electrolytes, fats, proteins, glucose (sugar), and enzymes. Some of the specific blood chemistry tests include a basic metabolic panel (BMP), a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP), and an electrolyte panel.</li></ul><p>If these tests show that you have <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, you will have tests that study the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> cells. These tests help your provider decide which treatment would be best for you. The tests may include:</p><ul><li>Genetic tests for genetic changes such in the BRCA and TP53 genes.</li><li>HER2 test. HER2 is a protein involved with cell growth. It is on the outside of all <span class="qt0">breast</span> cells. If your <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> cells have more HER2 than normal, they can grow more quickly and spread to other parts of the body.</li><li>An estrogen and progesterone receptor test. This test measures the amount of estrogen and progesterone (hormones) receptors in <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> tissue. If there are more receptors than normal, the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is called estrogen and/or progesterone receptor positive. This type of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> may grow more quickly.</li></ul><p>Another step is staging the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. Staging involves doing tests to find out whether the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> has spread within the <span class="qt0">breast</span> or to other parts of the body. The tests may include other diagnostic imaging tests and a sentinel lymph node biopsy. This biopsy is done to see whether the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> has spread to the lymph nodes.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>?<p>Treatments for <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> include:</p><ul><li>Surgery such as 
	<ul><li>A <span class="qt0">mastectomy</span>, which removes the whole <span class="qt0">breast</span></li><li>A lumpectomy to remove the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> and some normal tissue around it, but not the <span class="qt0">breast</span> itself</li></ul>
</li><li>Radiation therapy</li><li>Chemotherapy</li><li>Hormone therapy, which blocks <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> cells from getting the hormones they need to grow</li><li>Targeted therapy, which uses drugs or other substances that attack specific <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> cells with less harm to normal cells</li><li>Immunotherapy</li></ul>Can <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> be prevented?<p>You may be able to help prevent <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> by making healthy lifestyle changes such as:</p><ul><li>Staying at a healthy weight</li><li>Limiting alcohol use</li><li>Getting enough exercise</li><li>Limiting your exposure to estrogen by 
	<ul><li>Breastfeeding your babies if you can</li><li>Limiting hormone therapy</li></ul>
</li></ul><p>If you are at high risk, your provider may suggest that you take certain medicines to lower the risk. Some women at very high risk may decide to get a <span class="qt0">mastectomy</span> (of their healthy <span class="qt0">breasts</span>) to prevent <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>It's also important to get regular mammograms. They may be able to identify <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> in the early stages, when it is easier to treat.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title">Mammography</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is a mammogram?<p>A mammogram is an x-ray picture of the <span class="qt0">breast</span>. Health care providers use mammograms to look for early signs of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> that can't be felt during a <span class="qt0">breast</span> exam. There are two types of mammograms: screening mammograms and diagnostic mammograms.</p>What is a screening mammogram?<p>A screening mammogram is a mammogram usually done for women who have no signs or symptoms of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. Regular screening mammograms can help reduce the number of deaths from <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> among women ages 40 to 74. This is because they can find <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> early and treatment can start earlier, maybe before it has spread.</p><p>But screening mammograms can also have risks. They can sometimes find something that looks abnormal but isn't <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. This leads to further testing and can cause you anxiety. Sometimes mammograms can miss <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> when it is there. It also exposes you to radiation. You should talk to your provider about the benefits and drawbacks of mammograms. Together, you can decide when to start and how often to have a mammogram.</p>What is a diagnostic mammogram?<p>A diagnostic mammogram takes a little longer to do than a screening mammogram. It's done for people who have a lump or other signs or symptoms of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. The signs can include <span class="qt0">breast</span> pain, thickening of the skin of the <span class="qt0">breast</span>, nipple discharge, or a change in <span class="qt0">breast</span> size or shape. But these signs can also be caused by a <span class="qt0">breast</span> condition that is benign (not <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>). A diagnostic mammogram may also be used if you have <span class="qt0">breast</span> implants or if there are other reasons it's difficult to view your <span class="qt0">breast</span> tissue.</p>How is a mammogram done?<p>When you have a mammogram, you stand in front of an x-ray machine. The person who takes the x-rays places your <span class="qt0">breast</span> between two plastic plates. The plates press your <span class="qt0">breast</span> and make it flat. This may be uncomfortable, but it helps get a clear picture.</p><p>You will get both <span class="qt0">breasts</span> x-rayed from the front and from the side. Afterwards, a radiologist (a doctor with special training) will read the mammogram. The doctor will look at the x-ray for early signs of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> or other problems. You will usually get the results within a few weeks, although it depends on the clinic or medical office that you went to. If your results are not normal, you should hear back earlier. Ask your provider when and how you will receive your results.</p>What happens if my mammogram is not normal?<p>An abnormal (not normal) mammogram does not always mean that there is <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. You will need to have additional mammograms, tests, or exams before your provider can tell for sure. You may also be referred to a <span class="qt0">breast</span> specialist or a surgeon. But it does not necessarily mean you have <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> or need surgery. You would see one of these doctors because they are experts in diagnosing <span class="qt0">breast</span> problems.</p></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/mastectomy.html">
      <content name="title"><span class="qt0">Mastectomy</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Lumpectomy</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is a <span class="qt0">mastectomy</span>?<p>A <span class="qt0">mastectomy</span> is surgery to remove part or all of the <span class="qt0">breast</span>. It's usually done to treat <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> by removing the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. A <span class="qt0">mastectomy</span> may be the first treatment option for some types of <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> or done after chemotherapy for other types. If you are at a very high risk for <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, sometimes a <span class="qt0">mastectomy</span> may be done to reduce your risk.</p>What are the different types of <span class="qt0">mastectomies</span>?<p>There are different types of <span class="qt0">mastectomies</span>. Each differs in the amount of <span class="qt0">breast</span> tissue and lymph nodes that are removed. Some types of <span class="qt0">breast</span> surgery remove the <span class="qt0">breast</span> skin and the nipple. Others may also remove nearby lymph nodes, which are part of your immune system and help protect your body from infection and disease.</p><p>Which surgery you have depends on the stage of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, the size of the <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tumor</span></span>, the size of the <span class="qt0">breast</span>, and whether the lymph nodes are involved.</p><p>Types of <span class="qt0">breast</span> surgery include:</p><ul><li>Total (simple) <span class="qt0">mastectomy</span> is the removal of all the <span class="qt0">breast</span> tissue and nipple of the <span class="qt0">breast</span> that has <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. Some lymph nodes under your arm may be removed and checked for <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</li><li>Modified radical <span class="qt0">mastectomy</span> is the removal of the <span class="qt0">breast</span> that has <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, including the nipple, areola (dark-colored skin around the nipple), skin over the <span class="qt0">breast</span>, most of the lymph nodes under the arm, and often the lining over the chest muscles.</li><li>Lumpectomy is <span class="qt0">breast</span>-sparing surgery. The <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tumor</span></span> and some normal <span class="qt0">breast</span> tissue around it are removed, but not the <span class="qt0">breast</span> itself. Some lymph nodes under your arm may be removed and checked for <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>. Part of the chest wall lining may also be removed if <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> is near it.</li></ul><p>No matter which <span class="qt0">breast</span> surgery you choose, you may also need other treatments. These could include radiation therapy, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, or targeted therapy.</p><p>You may choose to have <span class="qt0">breast</span> reconstruction to rebuild your <span class="qt0">breast</span> at the same time as the <span class="qt0">mastectomy</span>, or it may be done later. Your health care provider may suggest waiting if radiation therapy is part of your treatment plan.</p><p>NIH: National <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> Institute</p></content>

      <content name="title"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Tumors</span></span> and Pregnancy</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Cancer</span></span> and Pregnancy</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Gestational Trophoblastic Disease</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Molar Pregnancy</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p><span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Tumors</span></span> during pregnancy are rare, but they can happen. <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">Tumors</span></span> can be either benign (not <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>) or malignant (<span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>). The most common <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancers</span></span> in pregnancy include <span class="qt0">breast</span> <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, thyroid <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>, cervical <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer, lymphoma, and melanoma.  Cancer</span></span> itself rarely harms the fetus, and some <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span> treatments are safe during pregnancy.  You and your health care provider will work together to find the best treatment.  Your choices will depend on how far along the pregnancy is, as well as the type, size, and stage of your <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">cancer</span></span>.</p><p>Another type of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tumor</span></span> that women can get is called a gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD). It happens when a fertilized egg doesn't become a fetus.  GTD is not always easy to find. It is usually benign, but some types can be malignant. The most common type of GTD is a molar pregnancy. In its early stages, it may look like a normal pregnancy. You should see your provider if you have vaginal bleeding (not menstrual bleeding).</p><p>Treatment depends on the type of <span class="qt1"><span class="qt2">tumor</span></span>, whether it has spread to other places, and your overall health.</p></content>
